etymology: Hebrew Elimelek, “my God is king,” the husband of Naomi and father of Mahlon and Chilion.
biblical_def: Elimelech was a man of Bethlehem-judah, an Ephrathite, the husband of Naomi and the father of Mahlon and Chilion. When a famine lay upon the land in the days when the judges ruled, Elimelech took his wife and his two sons and went to sojourn in the country of Moab, leaving the place of bread and the inheritance of the LORD for a foreign land (Ruth 1:1–2). There he died, and Naomi was left with her two sons (Ruth 1:3); and the sons also died, so that the woman was bereft of both her husband and her children in a strange country. Yet the LORD wove redemption out of this sorrow: when Naomi returned, Boaz the near kinsman bought all that had been Elimelech’s and married Ruth, raising up the name of the dead upon his inheritance (Ruth 4:9–10), and from that line came David and at last the Christ. Elimelech’s name, “my God is king,” is a quiet rebuke to his own course, for in turning from Bethlehem to Moab he sought bread where the LORD was not owned as king. His story warns that flight from the place of God’s appointment in the day of trial may lead a family into deeper loss, yet it also shows that God can redeem even the wreckage left by a man’s failing faith.
webster_summary: A man of Bethlehem, husband of Naomi, who went to Moab in famine and died there; ancestor in the line of David.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; his life warns against forsaking the place of God’s appointment in the day of trial.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the irony of Elimelech’s name against his course. “My God is king,” yet he fled the house of bread for the fields of Moab when famine came, seeking provision where the LORD was not honoured. The man whose name confessed God’s kingship acted as though God could not provide in Bethlehem. His story warns the believer not to flee the place of God’s appointment when trial comes, as if the Lord’s hand were shortened.

Yet Elimelech’s account is finally a testimony to redemption. Out of the loss of his house, through the faith of Ruth and the kindness of Boaz, the LORD raised up the line of David and the lineage of the Messiah. God is able to redeem even the wreckage left by a man’s failing faith, and to weave the sorrows of a bereaved family into the story of the world’s salvation.

etymology: Hebrew Machlon, perhaps “sickly” or “infirmity,” the elder son of Elimelech and the first husband of Ruth.
biblical_def: Mahlon was the elder son of Elimelech and Naomi, who went with his parents from Bethlehem to sojourn in Moab during the famine (Ruth 1:2). There he took to wife Ruth the Moabitess, and there, after about ten years, he died, as did his brother Chilion, leaving their mother bereft of husband and sons in a foreign land (Ruth 1:4–5). Though Mahlon died without offspring, his name was not blotted out: when Boaz redeemed the inheritance, he declared, “Moreover Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of Mahlon, have I purchased to be my wife, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance, that the name of the dead be not cut off from among his brethren” (Ruth 4:10). Thus the law of the kinsman-redeemer preserved Mahlon’s name in Israel, for the child born to Boaz and Ruth was reckoned to continue the line of the dead. His name, which seems to mean “sickly,” may hint at the frailty that brought him to an early grave far from home. Mahlon’s brief story witnesses the tender provision of God’s law for the widow and the dead, and the grace by which a Moabite widow’s husband became, through redemption, an ancestor of David and of the Lord Jesus Christ.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the gracious provision of the kinsman-redeemer for the dead. Mahlon died childless, yet his name was not cut off, for Boaz purchased Ruth to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance. The law of God cared for the widow and preserved the line of the departed; redemption reached even into the grave to keep a man’s name alive in Israel.

Mahlon’s marriage to a Moabitess, and the redemption that followed, also displays the wideness of God’s mercy. Ruth, a daughter of Moab, became through Mahlon and then Boaz an ancestress of David and of Christ. The gospel was foreshadowed in this Bethlehem household: a redeemer taking to himself a stranger and bringing her into the inheritance and the line of the promise.

etymology: Hebrew Kilyon, perhaps “pining” or “wasting away,” the younger son of Elimelech and the husband of Orpah.
biblical_def: Chilion was the younger son of Elimelech and Naomi, who went with his family from Bethlehem into the country of Moab when the famine drove them out (Ruth 1:2). There he married Orpah, one of the women of Moab, and there he died, together with his brother Mahlon, leaving their mother Naomi alone in a strange land, stripped of husband and sons (Ruth 1:4–5). His wife Orpah, unlike Ruth, turned back at the parting to her own people and her gods (Ruth 1:14–15). When Boaz redeemed the family inheritance, he bought all that had been Chilion’s as well as Mahlon’s and Elimelech’s, of the hand of Naomi (Ruth 4:9). His name, which seems to mean “pining” or “wasting away,” stands beside his brother’s “sickly,” as if the very names of the two sons foretold their early graves. Chilion is remembered chiefly in contrast: his widow Orpah went back, while Mahlon’s widow Ruth clave to Naomi and to the God of Israel, and entered the lineage of the Messiah. His brief story marks the parting of two ways, where one Moabitess returned to her idols and the other pressed on to the living God.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; his story marks the parting of two ways at the borders of Moab.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover lies in the contrast between the two widows of Elimelech’s sons. Chilion’s widow Orpah, having wept and kissed Naomi, turned back to her people and her gods; Mahlon’s widow Ruth clave to Naomi and to the LORD. The same parting hour found one returning to the idols and the other pressing on to the living God. Many come near to the kingdom and turn back; the question is whether one cleaves to the LORD or returns to the world.

Chilion’s name, “pining” or “wasting,” set beside his brother’s “sickly,” reminds the reader of the frailty of man and the certainty of death, even in the prime of life and far from home. Yet the LORD redeemed the inheritance of the dead, showing that His covenant mercy outlasts the graves of men and reaches to the generations after them.

etymology: Hebrew Orpah, perhaps “neck” or “she who turns the back,” the Moabite wife of Chilion.
biblical_def: Orpah was a woman of Moab, the wife of Chilion the son of Elimelech and Naomi (Ruth 1:4). When her husband and his brother had died, and Naomi resolved to return to Bethlehem, Orpah set out with her, weeping; but at Naomi’s urging that the young widows return to their mothers’ houses, Orpah lifted up her voice and wept, kissed her mother-in-law, and went back to her people and her gods (Ruth 1:14). “Behold,” Naomi said to Ruth, “thy sister in law is gone back unto her people, and unto her gods: return thou after thy sister in law” (Ruth 1:15). But Ruth clave unto Naomi and would not turn back. Orpah is remembered forever in contrast to Ruth: both began the journey, both wept, both were urged to return; but Orpah turned back to Moab and its idols, and is heard of no more, while Ruth pressed on to the God of Israel and became an ancestress of David and of Christ. Her name itself, linked to the neck or the turning of the back, fits her parting. Orpah stands as a solemn type of those who come near to the people of God and to the borders of faith, yet draw back, preferring the familiar gods of their own country to the living LORD.
webster_summary: The Moabite wife of Chilion, who wept but turned back to her people and her gods, in contrast to Ruth.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; she is a type of those who come near to faith yet draw back.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the warning of Orpah’s turning back. She wept, she kissed, she set out on the road; outwardly her affection seemed as great as Ruth’s. Yet when the cost was counted, she returned to her people and her gods, while Ruth pressed on. Many come near to the kingdom of God with tears and good beginnings, yet draw back to the world. The Scripture honours not the one who starts but the one who cleaves to the end.

Orpah and Ruth together teach that natural ties and warm feelings are not saving faith. Both were Moabitesses, both married into the same household, both wept at the parting; but one returned to Chemosh and one embraced the LORD. The dividing line was not blood or sentiment but the cleaving of the heart to the God of Israel. “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1Jn 2:19) is the abiding lesson of the woman who turned back.

etymology: Hebrew Achino’am, “my brother is delight” or “pleasant,” the name of Saul’s wife and of a wife of David.
biblical_def: Ahinoam was the name of two women in the days of the early monarchy. The first was the daughter of Ahimaaz, the wife of Saul the first king and mother of Jonathan and his brethren (1Sa 14:50). The second, more often named, was Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, whom David took to wife in the days of his wandering; she and Abigail were both his wives, and together they shared his hardships (1Sa 25:43). When the Amalekites burned Ziklag and carried off the families of David and his men, Ahinoam was among the captives, and David recovered her and all the rest by the help of the LORD (1Sa 30:5, 18). She bore David his firstborn, Amnon, in Hebron (2Sa 3:2). The name Ahinoam, “my brother is delight” or “pleasantness,” was borne in both a house that fell and a house that rose: Saul’s line passed away, while David’s endured to the Christ. Ahinoam the Jezreelitess shared the perils of David’s exile and the joy of his kingdom, a quiet witness to the women who bore the trials of the LORD’s anointed in the years before his throne was established.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the quiet endurance of those who shared the hardships of the LORD’s anointed before his glory. Ahinoam the Jezreelitess followed David through his wandering, was carried captive from Ziklag, and was restored by the hand of God; she bore the perils of exile and lived to see the kingdom. The Scripture honours such hidden faithfulness in the household of the king.

The name Ahinoam, borne in both Saul’s house and David’s, also marks the divergence of the two lines. Saul’s house, for all its early promise, fell under the judgment of God; David’s house, though chastened, endured to bring forth the Christ. The same name in two houses witnesses that lineage and outward standing do not determine a family’s end, but the LORD’s choice and a heart after Him.

etymology: Hebrew Ner, “a lamp” or “light,” the father of Abner and kinsman of Saul.
biblical_def: Ner was a man of Benjamin, the son of Abiel, the father of Abner who was captain of Saul’s host, and near kin to Saul the king (1Sa 14:51). The Scripture names him in tracing the house from which both the first king of Israel and his great captain sprang: “Kish was the father of Saul; and Ner the father of Abner was the son of Abiel” (1Sa 14:51), so that Kish and Ner were brethren, sons of Abiel, and Saul and Abner were thus of one kindred. The Chronicles preserve the genealogy of this Benjamite house among the records of the tribe (1Ch 8:33; 9:39). Ner himself does little in the narrative; his significance is in his son Abner, the strong arm of Saul’s kingdom, and in the lamp-like name he bore. “Ner” means “a lamp,” and the figure of the lamp runs through the story of the kingship: the LORD promised David a lamp that should not be put out, but the lamp of Saul’s house was at last extinguished for its unfaithfulness. Ner stands quietly at the head of a house that rose high and fell hard, a reminder that the lamp of a family is kept burning not by noble descent but by the favour and faithfulness of God.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is hidden in the meaning of Ner’s name. “Ner” means a lamp, and the lamp is a recurring figure for the continuance of a house. The LORD promised David a lamp that should never be put out; but the lamp of Saul’s house, despite its noble Benjamite descent, was extinguished for unfaithfulness. A family’s light is kept burning not by lineage but by the favour and faithfulness of God.

Ner, standing at the head of the house that produced both Saul and Abner, also reminds the reader that natural kinship does not bind men to one cause. Saul and Abner were of one blood, yet Abner long upheld Saul’s falling house against the anointed David, and died at last in the strife of the kingdoms. The ties of flesh are no sure guide; the heart must cleave to the LORD’s appointed and not to the failing house of man.

etymology: Hebrew Qish, perhaps “a bow” or “snare,” the father of Saul the first king of Israel.
biblical_def: Kish was a Benjamite, the son of Abiel, “a mighty man of power,” the father of Saul the first king of Israel (1Sa 9:1). His place in the sacred history begins with a homely errand: the asses of Kish were lost, and he sent his son Saul with a servant to seek them (1Sa 9:3). That search, ordered by the providence of God, brought Saul to Samuel the prophet, who anointed him king over Israel; so a lost herd of asses became the occasion of a kingdom. Kish was of the smallest tribe and of a humble family, as Saul himself confessed (1Sa 9:21), that the exalting of his son might be plainly the work of God and not of human greatness. After the tragic end of Saul and Jonathan, their bones were at last gathered and buried in the sepulchre of Kish their father in Zelah of Benjamin (2Sa 21:14). Kish, “a bow” by the sense of his name, is remembered as the father from whose ordinary household God drew the first king of His people. His story witnesses that the LORD raises men to high place from obscure beginnings, by the turning of small providences, that the glory may be His.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; his story shows God raising men to high place by small providences.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the providence that turned a lost herd of asses into a kingdom. Kish sent his son on a homely errand, and the LORD used that errand to bring Saul to Samuel and to the throne. God governs the smallest things of His people’s lives and bends them to His great purposes; nothing is too trivial for His ordering hand.

Kish’s humble Benjamite household also teaches that the LORD exalts from obscurity, that the glory may be His. Saul confessed himself of the smallest tribe and the least of families; his elevation was plainly God’s doing, not the fruit of human greatness. That the first king began so well and ended so badly is a further warning that high beginnings must be matched by a faithful heart, or the throne becomes a judgment.

etymology: Hebrew Avi’el, “God is my father” or “my father is God,” the ancestor of Saul and of Abner.
biblical_def: Abiel was a Benjamite, the head of the house from which both Saul the first king and Abner his captain descended. He was the father of Kish, who was the father of Saul; and the father of Ner, who was the father of Abner (1Sa 9:1; 14:51). Thus from the one house of Abiel sprang both the throne and the sword of the first kingdom: Saul who wore the crown, and Abner who upheld it in war. Abiel himself does nothing in the narrative; he is named only as the root of the family tree. Yet his name is a confession that towers over the history of his descendants: “God is my father.” The house that bore so godly a name rose to the highest place in Israel and then fell under the judgment of God, for Saul forsook the LORD and Abner long resisted His anointed. The name Abiel preached a truth the house failed to keep, that the LORD is the true Father of His people, to be honoured and obeyed above the ties of blood and the ambitions of the throne. Abiel stands at the head of his line as a silent witness that a godly name is no substitute for a faithful heart in the generations that follow.
webster_summary: A Benjamite, the common ancestor of Saul and of Abner; his name means “God is my father.”
webster_full: ABIEL, a Benjamite, the head of the house of Saul and Abner.
He was the father of Kish, the father of Saul (1Sa 9:1).
He was also the father of Ner, the father of Abner (1Sa 14:51).
From his one house sprang both the throne and the captain of the first kingdom.
His name signifies “God is my father.”
scriptures: Now there was a man of Benjamin, whose name was Kish, the son of Abiel, the son of Zeror, the son of Bechorath, the son of Aphiah, a Benjamite, a mighty man of power.
And Kish was the father of Saul; and Ner the father of Abner was the son of Abiel.
And Saul answered and said, Am not I a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel? and my family the least of all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? wherefore then speakest thou so to me?
And Ner begat Kish, and Kish begat Saul, and Saul begat Jonathan, and Malchishua, and Abinadab, and Eshbaal.
corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; his godly name witnesses that lineage cannot supply a faithful heart.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the contrast between Abiel’s name and his house’s end. “God is my father,” the name confessed; yet the line that bore it rose to the throne and fell under judgment, for Saul forsook the LORD. A godly name and a godly ancestry are precious, but they do not pass faith down the generations like an heirloom; each soul must own God as Father for himself.

Abiel, the one root of both Saul and Abner, also teaches that natural unity does not make spiritual unity. The same house gave Israel a king who disobeyed and a captain who long withstood the LORD’s anointed. Blood bound them together, but neither cleaved faithfully to God. The ties of family are a gift, but they are no guarantee of grace; the heart, not the bloodline, must be set on the LORD.
roots_summary: The name joins avi, “my father,” with El, “God,” confessing God as Father.
roots_lines: Abiel — Hebrew Avi’el, “God is my father.”

usage: Like Abiel’s house, a godly name and ancestry cannot supply a faithful heart to the generations.
Abiel teaches that natural kinship does not make spiritual unity before God.
The name “God is my father” must be owned by each soul, not merely inherited.

etymology: Hebrew Armoni, “of the palace” or “belonging to the citadel,” a son of Saul by Rizpah.
biblical_def: Armoni was one of the two sons whom Rizpah the daughter of Aiah bore to Saul, the brother of a Mephibosheth distinct from the son of Jonathan (2Sa 21:8). His brief and sorrowful place in Scripture comes in the days of David, when a three-year famine lay upon the land, and the LORD revealed that it was for the bloodguilt of Saul, who had slain the Gibeonites in his zeal, breaking the oath Israel had sworn to them in the days of Joshua. When David asked the Gibeonites what atonement they would have, they required that seven of Saul’s sons be delivered up; and the king took Armoni and his brother, with five sons of Merab, and gave them to the Gibeonites, who hanged them before the LORD (2Sa 21:8–9). Then Rizpah their mother took sackcloth and spread it upon the rock, and watched over the bodies of her sons from the beginning of harvest until the rain fell, suffering neither the birds nor the beasts to touch them, until the king was moved to gather the bones of Saul’s house for honourable burial (2Sa 21:10–14). Armoni’s death is a hard chapter, witnessing the dreadful seriousness of a broken oath and the long reach of a king’s sin upon his house.
webster_summary: A son of Saul by Rizpah, given to the Gibeonites to expiate Saul’s breach of Israel’s oath.
webster_full: ARMONI, a son of Saul by Rizpah the daughter of Aiah (2Sa 21:8).
His name signifies “of the palace” or “belonging to the citadel.”
He was delivered to the Gibeonites to expiate Saul’s bloodguilt.
He was hanged before the LORD with six others of Saul’s house (2Sa 21:9).
His mother Rizpah watched over the bodies until the rain fell (2Sa 21:10).
scriptures: But the king took the two sons of Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, whom she bare unto Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth; and the five sons of Michal the daughter of Saul, whom she brought up for Adriel the son of Barzillai the Meholathite:

And he delivered them into the hands of the Gibeonites, and they hanged them in the hill before the LORD: and they fell all seven together, and were put to death in the days of harvest, in the first days, in the beginning of barley harvest.

And Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth, and spread it for her upon the rock, from the beginning of harvest until water dropped upon them out of heaven, and suffered neither the birds of the air to rest on them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night.

Then there was a famine in the days of David three years, year after year; and David enquired of the LORD. And the LORD answered, It is for Saul, and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites.
corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; his death witnesses the seriousness of a broken oath and a king’s far-reaching sin.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dreadful seriousness with which God regards a broken oath. Israel had sworn to spare the Gibeonites; Saul, in zeal that was not according to knowledge, slew them, and the guilt lay upon his house until it was expiated. The LORD held the nation accountable for a covenant broken generations before. Vows sworn in His name are not trifles; He requires that men keep them.

Armoni’s death, and Rizpah’s long vigil over her sons, also display the far reach of a ruler’s sin upon those who come after him. The children suffered for the father’s bloodguilt, and a mother kept her grievous watch upon the rock. The narrative is hard, yet it teaches that sin in high places is no private matter; its bitter harvest falls upon a whole house, and only a true atonement can turn away the wrath.
roots_summary: The name means “of the palace” or “belonging to the citadel,” fitting a son of the king’s house.

etymology: Hebrew Gera, perhaps “a grain” or “sojourning,” an ancestral name in the tribe of Benjamin.
biblical_def: Gera was a name borne in the tribe of Benjamin from its earliest generations, for Gera is numbered among the sons of Benjamin who went down into Egypt (Gen 46:21), and the name recurs in the genealogies of the tribe (1Ch 8:3, 5, 7). Two famous Benjamites are called sons of Gera, and they stand in sharpest contrast. The first is Ehud the son of Gera, the left-handed deliverer whom the LORD raised up when Israel cried unto Him under the oppression of Eglon king of Moab; Ehud slew the tyrant and freed the land, and it had rest fourscore years (Judg 3:15). The second is Shimei the son of Gera, the man of the house of Saul who came forth cursing as David fled from Absalom, casting stones and dust at the LORD’s anointed in the day of his affliction (2Sa 16:5). Thus the one name of Gera was father to a deliverer and to a reviler, to a man who saved Israel and a man who cursed her king. Gera stands as a witness that a single house may bring forth both the faithful and the faithless, and that men are not measured by the name they inherit but by the heart they bear before the LORD.
webster_summary: A Benjamite ancestral name; father of Ehud the deliverer and of Shimei who cursed David.
webster_full: GERA, an ancestral name in the tribe of Benjamin.
Gera was among the sons of Benjamin who came into Egypt (Gen 46:21).
Ehud the son of Gera was the deliverer who slew Eglon of Moab (Judg 3:15).
Shimei the son of Gera cursed David in his flight (2Sa 16:5).
The name recurs in the genealogies of Benjamin (1Ch 8:3).

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; the name witnesses that one house may bring forth both the faithful and the faithless.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the contrast of the two sons of Gera. From the one Benjamite name came Ehud, a deliverer raised up by the LORD to free Israel, and Shimei, a reviler who cursed the LORD’s anointed in his affliction. A single house may bring forth both the faithful and the faithless; men are not measured by the name they inherit but by the heart they bear before God.

Gera’s line also illustrates how the same tribe and stock may serve very different ends in the providence of God. Benjamin gave Israel both her first king and her great deliverers, and also some of her bitterest opponents of the throne of David. The diversity within one house is a standing rebuke to all confidence in lineage; grace is not hereditary, and each generation must turn to the LORD for itself.
roots_summary: The name perhaps means “a grain” or “sojourning,” an old Benjamite name of several bearers.
